common_name: Encore Autumn Rouge Azalea (Reblooming Red-Violet Semi-Double Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4-6 hours of direct sun for reliable fall rebloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with several hours of direct sun for the best fall rebloom. Autumn Rouge produces semi-double flowers in a rich, saturated red-violet color, opening in a heavy spring flush and recurring through summer and fall on a medium-sized, well-branched shrub. Its bold flower color makes it a strong focal point among the cooler pinks and lavenders common in older azalea plantings. Like all Encore azaleas it needs more direct sun than traditional shade-azaleas to rebloom dependably, and benefits from an acid-based fertilizer application after the spring flush to fuel the later bloom cycles. Prune, if needed, right after the spring flush to avoid removing developing summer and fall buds.

common_name: Encore Autumn Angel Azalea (Reblooming Dwarf White Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4-6 hours of direct sun for reliable fall rebloom; its dwarf, spreading habit suits small beds, edging, and containers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with several hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom. Autumn Angel is one of the smallest Encore azaleas, staying under 18 inches tall with a low, spreading habit, and bears clean single white flowers in a heavy spring flush with lighter repeat bloom in summer and fall. Its diminutive size fits foundation edges, small beds, rock gardens, and large containers where full-size azaleas would quickly outgrow the space. As with all Encore azaleas, more direct sun than traditional shade azaleas produces the strongest rebloom, and an acid-based fertilizer applied after the spring flush supports the later flower cycles. Light shaping right after spring bloom keeps the compact form tidy without sacrificing developing buds.

common_name: Encore Autumn Starlite Azalea (Reblooming Dwarf Lavender-Pink Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4-6 hours of direct sun for reliable fall rebloom; its compact, mounding form works well in small beds and containers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with several hours of direct sun for the best fall rebloom. Autumn Starlite bears pale lavender-pink single flowers over a compact, mounding plant that stays smaller than most Encore selections, blooming heavily in spring with lighter repeat flushes through summer and fall. Its soft coloring and small scale make it useful for foundation plantings, small mixed borders, and mass plantings where a subtler color and tighter habit are wanted. Like other Encore azaleas it reblooms best with more direct sun than traditional shade azaleas receive, and an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush helps fuel later bloom. Shape lightly right after spring flowering to avoid cutting off developing summer and fall buds.

common_name: Little Rascal Gardenia (Compact Cold-Hardy Fragrant Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Rascal is a smaller-growing sport of Frostproof gardenia and fits tighter foundation spaces and large containers.

directions: Little Rascal is a compact Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia selected as a smaller-growing counterpart to the popular Frostproof, holding the same reliably cold-hardy, disease-resistant reputation on a tighter, more rounded frame that fits foundation beds and large containers where standard gardenia eventually grows too large. Its classic, intensely fragrant double white flowers open over a long stretch from late spring into summer against glossy dark evergreen foliage. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade — a little afternoon shade in the Deep South helps prevent leaf scorch and reduces whitefly pressure, the most common gardenia pest. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and after the main bloom flush, and prune, if needed, right after flowering since buds for next year form on the current season's growth.
